title: Cellulitis, erysipelas and skin abscess (adult)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Separate non-purulent cellulitis (streptococcal: beta-lactam, 5 days, extend only if not improving) from abscess (incision and drainage; MRSA-active antibiotic only with systemic signs or risk factors), and exclude necrotising infection early.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Cellulitis: acute, spreading, poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, swelling and tenderness, usually of one lower limb. Erysipelas: raised, sharply demarcated, bright red plaque on the face or leg.
Purulent infection (abscess, furuncle, carbuncle): fluctuant tender swelling or pus. Bedside ultrasound finds an occult collection.

Severity (IDSA 2014): mild, no systemic signs; moderate, systemic signs (temperature above 38°C or below 36°C, heart rate above 90, respiratory rate above 24, WBC above 12,000 or below 4,000 cells/mm3); severe, failed oral therapy, hypotension, organ dysfunction, bullae or skin sloughing, or immunocompromise.

Necrotising infection red flags: pain out of proportion, hard wooden induration beyond the erythema, bullae, skin necrosis or anaesthesia, crepitus, rapid spread, systemic toxicity. This is a surgical emergency.
Mimics: bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis (venous stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis); also consider DVT, gout, septic arthritis and bursitis.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Mild cellulitis needs no routine tests. Mark and date the edge of the erythema.
CBC, creatinine, CRP and blood cultures for moderate or severe infection, and always with malignancy on chemotherapy, neutropenia, severe immunodeficiency, animal bites or water immersion injuries.
Culture pus from drained abscesses to guide MRSA therapy.
Check glucose (undiagnosed diabetes) and look for the portal of entry: tinea pedis, fissures, ulcers, trauma, lymphoedema.
Suspected necrotising infection: do not wait for imaging; surgical exploration is diagnostic.

sections.title: Non-purulent cellulitis and erysipelas
items: Mild (oral): cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 625 mg (500/125) every 8 hours (ICMR 2022). Penicillin allergy: clindamycin 300 to 450 mg every 6 to 8 hours.
Moderate (IV): cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily, or clindamycin 600 mg IV every 8 hours; switch to oral once improving.

Add MRSA cover only with penetrating trauma, injection drug use, MRSA colonisation or infection elsewhere, purulence, or SIRS (IDSA 2014). Co-trimoxazole and doxycycline do not reliably cover streptococci, so combine them with a beta-lactam for cellulitis.
Severe or rapidly progressive (immunocompromise, hypotension, suspected deeper infection): vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 to 8 hours, with urgent surgical review.
Duration: 5 days, extended only if not improved (IDSA 2014; ICMR 5 to 7 days). Redness can look worse in the first 24 to 48 hours despite effective therapy.
Elevate the limb, treat tinea pedis and oedema, and give analgesia.

sections.title: Abscess, furuncle and carbuncle
items: Incision and drainage is the main treatment. A simple abscess without systemic signs usually needs no antibiotic.

Add an antibiotic after drainage for systemic signs, extensive surrounding cellulitis, multiple lesions, rapid progression, immunocompromise, diabetes, extremes of age, face, hand or genital site, or failed drainage.

Oral MRSA-active options for 5 to 10 days: co-trimoxazole 1 to 2 double-strength (160/800 mg) tablets twice daily, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, or clindamycin 300 to 450 mg every 6 to 8 hours. Use cephalexin if MSSA is confirmed.
Severe or toxic: drain plus IV vancomycin, or linezolid 600 mg IV or orally every 12 hours.
Recurrent abscesses: culture, look for pilonidal disease or hidradenitis, and consider decolonisation with nasal mupirocin twice daily for 5 days plus daily chlorhexidine washes.

sections.title: Escalate
items: Suspected necrotising fasciitis: immediate surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam (or a carbapenem), clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV every 8 hours for toxin suppression, and vancomycin or linezolid.
Periorbital swelling with proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement or reduced vision: treat as orbital cellulitis with urgent CT and ophthalmology review.
No improvement after 48 to 72 hours of appropriate therapy: reconsider the diagnosis and look for an abscess, MRSA, or deeper infection (pyomyositis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis).
Freshwater or seawater wound infections (Aeromonas, Vibrio): ICMR 2022 advises ciprofloxacin plus doxycycline; get early surgical review because they can become necrotising.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Diabetes with a foot wound: assess as diabetic foot infection (probe to bone, X-ray) and follow a diabetic foot protocol.
Pregnancy: cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and cefazolin are suitable. Avoid doxycycline; avoid co-trimoxazole in the first trimester and near term.

Recurrent cellulitis (3 to 4 episodes a year despite treating predisposing factors): phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) 250 mg or erythromycin 250 mg orally twice daily, or benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM every 2 to 4 weeks (IDSA 2014).
Chronic leg oedema or lymphoedema: compression once the acute infection settles reduces recurrence.
Facial cellulitis: use amoxicillin-clavulanate to cover sinus and dental organisms.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating bilateral red legs or venous stasis dermatitis as cellulitis.
Routine MRSA cover for typical non-purulent cellulitis.
Antibiotics without drainage for an abscess.
Missing early necrotising infection: pain out of proportion to the skin findings is the key clue.

drugs.name: Clindamycin
drugs.dose: 300 to 450 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours; 600 mg IV every 8 hours (600 to 900 mg in necrotising infection)
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy; toxin suppression. C. difficile risk; check local streptococcal and staphylococcal resistance.

drugs.name: Co-trimoxazole
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 double-strength (160/800 mg) tablets orally twice daily
drugs.notes: MRSA; purulent infection. Weak streptococcal cover.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.dose: 15 to 20 mg/kg IV every 8 to 12 hours (IDSA 2014: 30 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses), adjusted to renal function and levels

drugs.name: Linezolid
drugs.dose: 600 mg IV or orally every 12 hours
drugs.notes: MRSA. Monitor platelets beyond 2 weeks; serotonergic drug interactions.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.notes: Severe or necrotising infection, with vancomycin or linezolid.
